audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Monday, June fifteenth, twenty twenty-six. Here's what matters today.

Let's start with AI, because the lead story this morning is genuinely alarming for anyone building a business or a consulting practice around AI tools.

Anthropic — the company behind the Claude models — had its most powerful products pulled offline by the Trump administration. The story, broken by Axios, is that Anthropic allegedly failed to honour a recent cyber executive order, and when administration officials felt the company wasn't taking it seriously, they acted. The quote from one source is blunt: "Everybody said Anthropic was a bad actor." What makes this story important isn't the politics — it's the operational lesson. If your clients, or your own work, are building on top of any of these foundation model providers, you now have documented evidence that access to those tools can be disrupted by a political disagreement in Washington. That's a material business continuity risk, and it's exactly the kind of thing a savvy AI marketing consultant should be raising with clients before it becomes their problem. The framing of "AI governance is now contact sport" isn't metaphor — it's a live case study that just played out this weekend.

Connected to that: TechCrunch has a piece this morning on what they're calling the AI layoff powder keg. The argument is that the displacement of tens of thousands of workers is happening at the exact same moment that a small cohort of AI insiders — the people building and selling these tools — is accumulating wealth at a scale that's hard to comprehend. What makes this combustible isn't just the inequality, it's the visibility of the inequality. People losing their jobs to automation can now watch the people who built the automation ring the bell on billion-dollar funding rounds. For Midya, this matters on two levels. First, as an AI-in-marketing specialist, you are going to be asked about this tension by clients — expect it in boardrooms, expect it in RFPs. Second, the backlash risk is real for brands seen as over-automating customer-facing functions without a human story to go with it. Getting ahead of that narrative is a consulting opportunity.

On the commerce media side, new data from Koddi shows that agentic AI is already reshaping how commerce media is bought, measured, and monetised — not in a theoretical future-state way, but right now, in a market that's already in motion. The key shift is that AI agents are beginning to make purchasing and bidding decisions autonomously, which breaks the traditional attribution models that most marketing teams still rely on. If you're working with retail or e-commerce clients, this is a conversation worth having immediately. The playbook for measuring ROI on paid media is being rewritten in real time.

Now to higher education, which has several threads this morning that are directly relevant to your consulting pipeline.

The biggest headline is that the University of Toronto has topped Oxford and Cambridge in a global research ranking. This is a significant reputational moment for Canadian higher education as a whole. It gives Canadian institutions — not just U of T — a powerful narrative to lean into when competing for international students, research funding, and global partnerships. For you, it's a conversation starter: any Canadian university you're in dialogue with right now has a fresh reason to think about how they're marketing their institutional prestige, and how they're differentiating themselves in a global field. That's your lane.

More urgently: Manitoba has shut down its student route to permanent residency. This is the latest in what is becoming a clear national pattern of provincial immigration retrenchment. Nova Scotia, Ontario, and now Manitoba have all tightened or eliminated pathways that used to make Canada an attractive long-term destination for international students — not just a place to study, but a place to build a life. Indian students are specifically cited as the most heavily affected group, given how prominently Manitoba featured in their post-graduation planning. For the institutions you're targeting as consulting clients, this is a five-alarm issue. Enrolment planning, international student marketing strategies, and the entire value proposition they pitch to prospective students from South and Southeast Asia is shifting underneath them. If you can walk into a meeting with a Canadian university and say "here's how I'd help you reframe your international student messaging in a tightened immigration environment" — that's a door opener right now.

Locally, Thompson Rivers University is getting some meaningful profile this morning. A minister toured a TRU sustainability project, and separately, there's a national feature about a TRU student rebuilding their career while helping rebuild a community — the kind of human-interest story that punches above its weight for institutional brand. For you, TRU is your backyard client. Ministerial attention on a sustainability project typically signals either incoming funding or a political priority that the institution is being used to demonstrate. Either way, it means there's momentum at TRU right now, and that momentum creates openings for external advisors. Worth a note to whoever you know there.

Also worth flagging: Nigeria has lifted its tuition remittance cap from fifteen thousand to twenty-five thousand dollars per semester for students studying abroad. On the surface this sounds positive — more Nigerian students could afford to send money to pay for degrees. But experts are quoted saying the bigger barriers remain visa access and finding funding in the first place. For Canadian universities actively recruiting in West Africa, this is a modest tailwind, but don't overweight it — the structural challenges haven't changed.

On the global front, two stories are worth your time this morning.

The US and Iran have reached a deal — and President Trump announced it over the weekend. Prime Minister Carney is heading to the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, with this as the backdrop. The BBC has a useful piece asking the practical question: how quickly could things actually normalise? The short answer from experts is: slowly. The economic aftershocks of the conflict — energy price volatility, supply chain disruptions, elevated insurance costs on shipping — don't evaporate with a handshake. Markets may be pricing in relief faster than the real economy can deliver it. For Canada, the bigger watch item at the G7 is how Carney manages the bilateral relationship with the US on trade and tariffs. A Canada-US alignment on Iran could create goodwill, but it doesn't automatically resolve the outstanding tariff disputes. Watch for any joint communiqué language coming out of Evian this week.

The Iran deal also has a direct implication for mortgage rates, which connects to the next section. With geopolitical risk receding and a Federal Reserve decision coming this week, analysts are asking how much downward pressure could hit yields — and by extension, fixed mortgage rates. More on that in a moment.

On the real estate front, this is actually a consequential week to be watching if you hold property in BC.

The combination of the Iran deal reducing geopolitical risk premium in bond markets, and the Fed's rate decision expected later this week, is creating a window where fixed mortgage rates could move meaningfully lower. HousingWire is tracking this closely. For your Sun Peaks, Langley, and Vancouver properties, the rate environment affects both carrying costs if you have variable exposure and the broader buyer demand picture if you're thinking about any disposition or refinancing decisions. Worth a conversation with your mortgage broker before the Fed announcement.

On the brokerage side, there's a piece this morning that's relevant to your eXp Realty interest and any brokerage consulting work. HousingWire has a sharp analysis on why top-producing agents leave — and the answer isn't usually money. They leave because they quietly outgrow their brokerage and start feeling invisible, or because a competitor offered them a more specific support structure at the right moment. The fix, the piece argues, is proactive retention conversations and removing operational friction before agents start looking. For eXp specifically, this is interesting because their model is structurally designed around agent autonomy and revenue sharing — which addresses some of these issues — but the "feeling invisible" problem doesn't disappear just because you have a good comp plan. Culture and coaching still matter, and that's a consulting conversation.

A couple of local stories from Kamloops worth noting this morning.

First, the fun one: Logan Stankoven and the Carolina Hurricanes won the Stanley Cup, and Stankoven is Kamloops-born — making him the first player from the city to lift the Cup since Mark Recchi back in 1991. That's over three decades. The city is celebrating, and rightfully so. Jordan Staal won the Conn Smythe as playoff MVP at age thirty-seven, the oldest recipient on record. A genuinely good sports story to start the week.

On a more sober note, Kamloops RCMP are seeking a suspect in a stabbing that occurred Sunday morning. Details are limited at this point, but it's worth awareness for local situational safety.

One longevity story this morning that clears the source bar and is worth your attention, particularly given the GLP-1 conversation that keeps surfacing.

Axios, citing health system reporting, flags that Medicare's new program providing GLP-1 weight-loss drugs — Wegovy, Zepbound, and similar — at fifty dollars a month is launching next month. The expectation is a massive surge in prescriptions from seniors who have wanted these drugs but couldn't afford them. The concern flagged by clinicians isn't the demand itself — it's that the system isn't prepared to provide the counselling, dosage management, and side-effect monitoring that make these drugs work safely. GLP-1s are not set-and-forget medications. The risk is that a wave of new patients gets prescribed these drugs in five-minute appointments without the wraparound support they need. For you personally: if you or family members are tracking GLP-1 options, the signal here is that access is improving dramatically, but the quality of the clinical experience may be getting worse at the same time. Choose your provider carefully.

That's your Monday briefing, Midya. The through-line today is governance and instability — whether that's AI platforms being pulled offline by political decisions, provincial immigration pathways closing without warning, or geopolitical deals creating rate volatility in your property market. The week ahead rewards people who are watching these second-order effects, not just the headlines. The Anthropic story in particular is worth sitting with: it's the clearest signal yet that your AI consulting thesis needs a governance and resilience layer built into it, not just a capability and strategy layer. Have a sharp week.
